label: Q19
topic: Short run vs long run, total product curve, diminishing returns
explain:
Slide 4 — time and inputs. A firm uses inputs (workers, land, machines) to make output.

  • Long run = the time period in which all inputs can be varied (changed).
  • Short run = the time period in which at least one input is fixed.
  • Tiny example: a café. Tomorrow it can hire one more barista (variable input), but it cannot build a bigger kitchen (fixed input). That is the short run. In two years it can also change the kitchen. That is the long run.
  • Total product curve = shows how output depends on the amount of the variable input (for example labor L), while the fixed input stays the same. On the graph: workers on the X axis, output on the Y axis.

Slide 8 — diminishing returns.

  • Diminishing returns to an input: you add more of one input, keep all other inputs fixed, and the marginal product of that input goes down.
  • The professor's short version: "Diminishing returns = Marginal product is decreasing."
  • The professor's math: Q = f(L) is an increasing function of L. Marginal production Q′ = f′(L) > 0, but Q″ = f″(L) < 0.
  • Meaning: f′(L) > 0 → each extra worker still adds output, so total product goes up. f″(L) < 0 → the amount each extra worker adds gets smaller, so the total product curve gets flatter.
  • Class numbers (George and Martha's farm, Week 6 slide 5): output 0, 19, 36, 51, 64, 75, 84, 91, 96. The marginal product of each new worker: 19, 17, 15, 13, 11, 9, 7, 5. All positive (f′ > 0), each one smaller (f″ < 0).
  • Why it happens: the fixed input (land) is shared by more and more workers. Two cooks in one small kitchen help a lot; the tenth cook mostly gets in the way.
question: (a) Define the short run and the long run. (b) What does the total product curve show? (c) What are diminishing returns to an input? Explain them with the production function Q = f(L) (use f′(L) and f″(L)).
answer:
(a) The long run is the time period in which all inputs can be varied. The short run is the time period in which at least one input is fixed (for example, the size of the farm or factory).

(b) The total product curve shows how the quantity of output depends on the quantity of the variable input (labor), for a given quantity of the fixed input.

(c) There are diminishing returns to an input when an increase in the quantity of that input, holding the levels of all other inputs fixed, leads to a decline in the marginal product of that input. In short: diminishing returns = marginal product is decreasing.

With the production function Q = f(L):

  • Total production Q = f(L) is an increasing function of L.
  • Marginal production Q′ = f′(L) > 0: one more worker still increases output.
  • But Q″ = f″(L) < 0: the marginal product falls as L rises, so the total product curve rises but becomes flatter.

Example: on George and Martha's farm the marginal product of labor is 19, 17, 15, 13, 11, 9, 7, 5 bushels. It is always positive, but it keeps falling, because more workers share the same fixed land.
memorize: Long run: ALL inputs variable. Short run: at least ONE input fixed.
Total product curve: output vs variable input, fixed input held constant.
Diminishing returns = marginal product is decreasing.
Q = f(L): f′(L) > 0 (TP rises) but f″(L) < 0 (TP gets flatter).

label: Q21–Q22
topic: Figure 7-8: MC, ATC, AVC, AFC curves at Ben's Boots
explain:
Slide 24 = Figure 7-8, "Marginal Cost and Average Cost Curves for Ben's Boots". One graph, four curves. X axis = quantity of boots (pairs, 0–10). Y axis = cost of a pair ($0–$250).

  • MC (red): a straight line going up, $12, $36, $60 … $228. Each extra pair costs $24 more than the one before (increasing marginal cost).
  • AFC = FC/Q (light purple): always falling, 108, 54, 36, 27 … 10.80. The fixed $108 is shared by more pairs.
  • AVC = VC/Q (purple): a rising straight line, $12 at 1 pair up to $120 at 10 pairs.
  • ATC = TC/Q = AFC + AVC (purple): U-shaped, 120, 78, 72, 75, 81.60 … 130.80.
  • Point M: MC crosses ATC at the bottom of the U, at 3 pairs and $72. The slide labels 3 pairs the "Minimum-cost output".

Why is ATC U-shaped? Two effects pull in opposite directions (Week 6 slide 23):

  • Spreading effect: more output shares the fixed cost → AFC falls → pushes ATC down.
  • Diminishing returns effect: more output needs more and more variable input → AVC rises → pushes ATC up.
  • At small output the spreading effect wins (ATC falls: 120 → 78 → 72). At large output diminishing returns wins (ATC rises: 72 → 75 → 81.60 …).

Why does MC cut ATC exactly at its minimum? Think of your class average height (professor's example, slide 28): if a new student is taller than the average, the average goes up; if shorter, it goes down. MC is the "new comer", ATC is the average.

  • 3rd pair: MC = $60 is below ATC at 2 pairs ($78) → ATC falls to (156 + 60)/3 = $72.
  • 4th pair: MC = $84 is above ATC at 3 pairs ($72) → ATC rises to (216 + 84)/4 = $75.
  • So ATC stops falling and starts rising exactly where MC = ATC: point M.
  • Professor's proof (slide 27): dATC/dQ = (1/Q)(MC − ATC). It is < 0 if MC < ATC, = 0 if MC = ATC (minimum), > 0 if MC > ATC.
question:
Q21. Look at Figure 7-8 for Ben's Boots. Name the four cost curves and describe their shapes. Why is the average total cost curve U-shaped?

Q22. Why does the marginal cost curve cross the average total cost curve at its lowest point M? What is the minimum-cost output for Ben's Boots, and what is the ATC there?
answer:
Q21. The four curves are:

  • MC (marginal cost): upward sloping, because of diminishing returns to the variable input (increasing marginal cost).
  • AFC (average fixed cost = FC/Q): always falling, because the fixed cost of $108 is divided by more pairs.
  • AVC (average variable cost = VC/Q): rising.
  • ATC (average total cost = TC/Q = AFC + AVC): U-shaped.

ATC is U-shaped because increasing output has two opposing effects. The spreading effect: the larger the output, the more units share the fixed cost, so AFC falls. The diminishing returns effect: the more output, the more variable input each extra unit needs, so AVC rises. At low output the spreading effect dominates and ATC falls. At high output the diminishing returns effect dominates and ATC rises. Example: from 1 to 2 pairs AFC falls by $54 but AVC rises by only $12, so ATC falls (120 → 78). From 3 to 4 pairs AFC falls by $9 but AVC rises by $12, so ATC rises (72 → 75).

Q22. An average goes down when the new unit is below the average, and goes up when the new unit is above it. ("For the average to be bigger, the new comer has to be greater than the average.")

  • If MC < ATC, ATC is falling.
  • If MC > ATC, ATC is rising.
  • So ATC is lowest where MC = ATC. That is point M, where MC crosses ATC.

Proof: dATC/dQ = d(TC/Q)/dQ = (MC·Q − TC)/Q² = (1/Q)(MC − ATC). This is 0 only when MC = ATC, so that is the minimum.

For Ben's Boots: the 3rd pair has MC = $60 < ATC(2) = $78, so ATC falls to $72; the 4th pair has MC = $84 > ATC(3) = $72, so ATC rises to $75. The minimum-cost output is 3 pairs, with minimum ATC = $72 (point M).
memorize: Four curves: MC (up), AFC (always down), AVC (up), ATC (U).
ATC = AFC + AVC. Spreading effect (AFC falls) vs diminishing returns effect (AVC rises).
MC < ATC → ATC falls; MC > ATC → ATC rises; MC = ATC → ATC minimum.
dATC/dQ = (1/Q)(MC − ATC).
Ben's Boots: minimum-cost output = 3 pairs, ATC = $72 (point M).

label: Q23
topic: Should I operate even with a loss? Shut-down rule P > AVC
explain:
Slide 11 — "Should I operate my business even if I get loss?"

Key idea: the fixed cost (rent, for example) must be paid even if you shut down. So if you close, your loss = FC = 1000. If you stay open, your loss = TR − VC − FC. Pick whichever loss is smaller.

CaseFCVCTCRevenueProfit if operateProfit if shut downTR − VCOperate?
a10002000300050002000−10003000Yes
b10003000400040000−10001000Yes
c1000400050004500−500−1000500Yes
d1000500060005000−1000−10000Maybe
e1000600070005500−1500−1000−500No
  • Case c (the slide's example): you lose 500 if you operate, but 1000 if you shut down. So you keep operating. Revenue (4500) pays all of VC (4000) and some of FC.
  • Case d: you lose 1000 either way → "Maybe" (indifferent). Revenue only just covers VC.
  • Case e: operating loses 1500, shutting down loses only 1000 → shut down. Revenue (5500) does not even cover VC (6000).

The rule on the slide: operate while loss from operating < fixed cost:

−(TR − VC − FC) < FC
⇒ TR − VC > 0
⇒ P·Q > Q·AVC      (TR = P·Q, VC = Q·AVC)
⇒ P > AVC

So in the short run: operate if P > AVC, even when there is a loss.
question: Using the table on the slide (cases a–e), should the firm keep operating in case c even though it makes a loss? Explain why, say what happens in cases d and e, and show that the business operating condition becomes P > AVC.
answer:
Yes, in case c the firm should keep operating. If it shuts down, it still has to pay the fixed cost of 1000, so its loss is 1000. If it operates, its loss is TR − TC = 4500 − 5000 = −500. Losing 500 is better than losing 1000. Revenue (4500) covers all of the variable cost (4000) and 500 of the fixed cost.

  • Case d: loss is 1000 whether it operates or not (TR = VC = 5000), so the firm is indifferent ("Maybe").
  • Case e: operating loses 1500 but shutting down loses only 1000 (TR 5500 < VC 6000), so the firm should shut down.
  • Cases a and b: profit is 2000 and 0, both better than −1000, so operate.

Operating condition: keep operating as long as the loss from operating is smaller than the fixed cost:

−(TR − VC − FC) < FC  ⇒  TR − VC > 0  ⇒  TR > VC
TR = P·Q and VC = Q·AVC  ⇒  P·Q > Q·AVC  ⇒  P > AVC

So the firm produces in the short run when price is above average variable cost, even if it makes a loss.
memorize: If you shut down, you still pay FC → loss = FC.
Operate while loss < FC, i.e. TR > VC.
Divide by Q: P > AVC → operate.
Case c: lose 500 by operating vs 1000 by closing → operate.
d: TR = VC → maybe; e: TR < VC → shut down.

label: Q24
explain:
Slide 15 = Table 7-4, "Summary of the Perfectly Competitive Firm's Profitability and Production Conditions". It has two halves. Two different price levels to compare with:

  • Break-even price = minimum ATC. Tells you: profit or loss? Enter or exit in the long run?
  • Shut-down price = minimum AVC. Tells you: produce or not in the short run?
Profitability condition (min ATC = break-even price)Result
P > minimum ATCFirm profitable. Entry into industry in the long run.
P = minimum ATCFirm breaks even. No entry into or exit from industry in the long run.
P < minimum ATCFirm unprofitable. Exit from industry in the long run.
Production condition (min AVC = shut-down price)Result
P > minimum AVCFirm produces in the short run. If P < minimum ATC, firm covers variable cost and some but not all of fixed cost. If P > minimum ATC, firm covers all variable cost and fixed cost.
P = minimum AVCFirm indifferent between producing in the short run or not. Just covers variable cost.
P < minimum AVCFirm shuts down in the short run. Does not cover variable cost.

Why two different prices? In the short run, fixed cost must be paid anyway, so only variable cost matters for "produce or not" (that is the slide 11 rule P > AVC). In the long run, nothing is fixed, so a firm stays only if it covers all costs (P ≥ min ATC).

Easy picture: min AVC is lower than min ATC. Price can be in three zones:

  • P above min ATC → profit, produce, new firms come in.
  • P between min AVC and min ATC → loss, but still produce in the short run (like case c on slide 11); exit in the long run.
  • P below min AVC → shut down now.

Example with Ben's Boots numbers (Week 6): min ATC = $72, min AVC = $12. At P = $50 the firm loses money but keeps producing in the short run, and leaves in the long run.
question: Summarize the perfectly competitive firm's profitability condition and production condition (Table 7-4). What are the break-even price and the shut-down price? What does the firm do in the short run and in the long run when P >, =, or < each of them?
answer:
The break-even price is the firm's minimum average total cost (the price where profit is zero). The shut-down price is its minimum average variable cost.

Profitability condition (compare P with min ATC) — long run:

  • P > min ATC: the firm is profitable; firms enter the industry in the long run.
  • P = min ATC: the firm breaks even; no entry or exit in the long run.
  • P < min ATC: the firm is unprofitable; firms exit in the long run.

Production condition (compare P with min AVC) — short run:

  • P > min AVC: the firm produces in the short run. If P < min ATC, it covers its variable cost and some, but not all, of its fixed cost (it makes a loss but loses less than by shutting down). If P > min ATC, it covers all variable and fixed cost.
  • P = min AVC: the firm is indifferent between producing or not; it just covers variable cost.
  • P < min AVC: the firm shuts down in the short run, because it cannot cover even its variable cost.

Reason: in the short run the fixed cost must be paid anyway, so the firm only needs P > AVC to produce. In the long run all costs can be avoided, so the firm stays only if P covers ATC.
memorize: Break-even price = min ATC → profit? entry/exit in LONG run.
Shut-down price = min AVC → produce? in SHORT run.
min AVC < P < min ATC: loss, but keep producing in short run; exit in long run.
P < min AVC: shut down now (can't cover variable cost).
P > min ATC: profit → entry; P = min ATC: no entry/exit.

label: Q25
topic: Midpoint method for price elasticity of demand
explain:
Slide 6 — the midpoint method. A way to compute percent change by dividing by the average (midpoint) of the start and end values, not by the start value.

(5-4)  % change in X = Change in X / Average value of X × 100

(5-5)                              (Q2 − Q1) / [(Q1 + Q2)/2]
       Price elasticity of demand = ---------------------------
                                   (P2 − P1) / [(P1 + P2)/2]
  • Why? With the normal method (divide by the starting value), going A → B and B → A gives two different answers (slide 5: 0.82 and 1.22).
  • The average of the two points is the same in both directions, so the midpoint method gives one answer both ways.
  • Use the absolute value (drop the minus sign). e > 1 elastic, e = 1 unit-elastic, e < 1 inelastic.
question:
(1) Using the midpoint method, compute the price elasticity of demand between A (P = $0.90, Q = 1,100) and B (P = $1.10, Q = 900). Show that A → B and B → A give the same answer and classify demand.

(2) Practice in the same style: the price rises from $20 (point A, Q = 50) to $30 (point B, Q = 30). Find the elasticity with the midpoint method, and compare it with the simple method in both directions.
answer:
(1) Slide data, midpoint method

  • Average Q = (1,100 + 900)/2 = 1,000. Change in Q = 200.
  • % change in Q = 200 / 1,000 × 100 = 20%.
  • Average P = (0.90 + 1.10)/2 = 1.00. Change in P = 0.20.
  • % change in P = 0.20 / 1.00 × 100 = 20%.
  • Elasticity = 20% / 20% = 1.00.

B → A uses the same averages (1,000 and 1.00), so it also gives 1.00. Demand is unit-elastic. Check: total revenue is $0.90 × 1,100 = $990 at A and $1.10 × 900 = $990 at B, unchanged, as unit-elastic demand predicts.

(2) Practice: $20 → $30, Q 50 → 30

% change in Q% change in PElasticity
Midpoint20 / 40 × 100 = 50%10 / 25 × 100 = 40%50 / 40 = 1.25
Simple, A → B20 / 50 × 100 = 40%10 / 20 × 100 = 50%40 / 50 = 0.80
Simple, B → A20 / 30 × 100 = 66.7%10 / 30 × 100 = 33.3%66.7 / 33.3 = 2.00

Midpoint averages: Q = (50 + 30)/2 = 40, P = (20 + 30)/2 = 25. The midpoint answer is 1.25 in both directions, so demand is elastic. The simple method gives 0.80 one way and 2.00 the other way. That is the problem the midpoint method solves. (Revenue check: $20 × 50 = $1,000 falls to $30 × 30 = $900 when price rises, which fits elastic demand.)
memorize: % change = change / AVERAGE of start and end × 100.
Same answer A→B and B→A.
Slide data: 20% / 20% = 1.00 → unit-elastic (revenue $990 both).
e > 1 elastic, = 1 unit, < 1 inelastic.

label: Q26
topic: Problem with simple % change: elasticity depends on direction
explain:
Slide 5 — "Some Problems in Calculating Elasticities". Data: Situation A: P = $0.90, Q = 1,100. Situation B: P = $1.10, Q = 900. The graph shows a downward-sloping demand curve with B higher and to the left of A.

Simple method (Week 5 slide 4): % change = change / starting value × 100. Elasticity = % change in Q / % change in P.

  • Going A → B, you divide by A's numbers (0.90 and 1,100).
  • Going B → A, you divide by B's numbers (1.10 and 900).
  • Different denominators → different answers: 0.82 vs 1.22. Same two points, same curve!
  • Worse: 0.82 < 1 looks inelastic, 1.22 > 1 looks elastic. The classification flips.
  • Fix: the midpoint method (slide 6), which gives 1.00 both ways.

Small slide typos: it writes "(= 18.1 / 22.22)" — exactly it is 18.18 / 22.22. And "(= 22.2 / 1.2)" should be 22.22 / 18.18. The final answers 0.82 and 1.22 are correct.
question: The price of a good rises from $0.90 (A, quantity demanded 1,100) to $1.10 (B, quantity demanded 900). Using the simple percent-change formula, compute the price elasticity of demand from A to B and from B to A. Why are the answers different, and how can this problem be fixed?
answer:
A → B (divide by A's values):

  • % change in price = 0.20 / 0.90 × 100 = 22.22%
  • % change in quantity = 200 / 1,100 × 100 = 18.18%
  • Elasticity = 18.18 / 22.22 = 0.82 (inelastic)

B → A (divide by B's values):

  • % change in price = 0.20 / 1.10 × 100 = 18.18%
  • % change in quantity = 200 / 900 × 100 = 22.22%
  • Elasticity = 22.22 / 18.18 = 1.22 (elastic)

Why different? The simple method divides each change by the starting value, and the starting value depends on the direction. So the same two points on the same demand curve give two elasticities, and even two different classifications (0.82 inelastic, 1.22 elastic).

Fix: use the midpoint method: divide by the average of the two values. % change in Q = 200 / 1,000 = 20%, % change in P = 0.20 / 1.00 = 20%, so elasticity = 1.00 in both directions (unit-elastic).
memorize: Cause: dividing by the STARTING value, which depends on direction.
Fix: midpoint method → 20% / 20% = 1.00.
Exact values: 9/11 and 11/9.

label: Q27

explain:
Slide 16 = Table 7-1, "Costs at Ben's Boots". Columns: quantity Q (pairs), fixed cost FC, variable cost VC, total cost TC = FC + VC, marginal cost MC = ΔTC/ΔQ.

  • FC = $108 at every quantity, even at 0 (it does not change with output).
  • TC = FC + VC. At Q = 0, TC = 108 + 0 = $108.
  • MC = ΔTC/ΔQ = how much TC goes up when you make one more pair. On the slide, MC numbers sit between rows (zig-zag lines), because MC is the change from one row to the next.

  • MC goes 12, 36, 60, 84 … rising by $24 each time. Each pair costs more than the one before = increasing marginal cost (slide 17), caused by diminishing returns.

The exam may also ask for averages (Week 6 slides 19–22): ATC = TC/Q, AFC = FC/Q, AVC = VC/Q, and the minimum-cost output.

label: Q28
topic: Ticket demand and supply schedules, supply shift, equilibrium
explain:
Three slides with the same hockey-ticket market.

  • Slide 6 (Figure 3-1, demand schedule): as price rises, quantity demanded falls (law of demand), so the demand curve slopes down. The professor's red warning: "In economics, the Y axis is always for the Price, and X axis is the quantity."
  • Slide 21 (Figure 3-5, supply schedule): as price rises, quantity supplied rises, so the supply curve slopes up.
  • Slide 22 (Figure 3-6, a decrease in supply): after the announcement, sellers offer 1,000 fewer tickets at every price. The whole supply curve shifts left from S1 to S2. The "after" column is exactly the slide 21 schedule.
PriceQd (slide 6)Qs before, S1 (slide 22)Qs after, S2 (slides 21/22)
$3505,0009,8008,800
$3006,0009,5008,500
$2508,0009,0008,000
$20011,0008,0007,000
$15015,0006,0005,000
$10020,0003,0002,000

How to use the numbers:

  • Equilibrium: the price where Qd = Qs.
  • Qs > Qd → surplus (price will fall). Qd > Qs → shortage (price will rise).
  • Shift vs movement: quantity changes at the same price → shift of the curve. Quantity changes because the price changed → movement along the curve.
question:
Use the demand schedule for tickets (Figure 3-1) and the supply schedules (Figures 3-5 and 3-6).

  1. Find the equilibrium price and quantity with the supply schedule of Figure 3-5 (= "after announcement").
  2. Find the surplus or shortage at $350 and at $150.
  3. By how much does supply decrease in Figure 3-6? Which way does the curve shift? What happens to the equilibrium price and quantity compared with the "before" supply S1?
  4. Is the change from (250, 9,000) to (250, 8,000) a shift or a movement? What about (250, 8,000) to (200, 7,000) on S2?
answer:
1. Equilibrium (D with S2 = Figure 3-5)

PriceQdQs (S2)Qs − QdResult
$3505,0008,800+3,800surplus
$3006,0008,500+2,500surplus
$2508,0008,0000equilibrium
$20011,0007,000−4,000shortage
$15015,0005,000−10,000shortage
$10020,0002,000−18,000shortage

Equilibrium price = $250, equilibrium quantity = 8,000 tickets (Qd = Qs = 8,000).

2. At $350: Qs − Qd = 8,800 − 5,000 = surplus of 3,800, so the price falls. At $150: Qd − Qs = 15,000 − 5,000 = shortage of 10,000, so the price rises.

3. At every price, after − before = −1,000 (9,800 → 8,800, 9,500 → 8,500, …, 3,000 → 2,000). Supply decreases by 1,000 tickets at each price, so the supply curve shifts left (S1 → S2).

  • With S1: at $250, Qs = 9,000 > Qd = 8,000 (surplus 1,000); at $200, Qs = 8,000 < Qd = 11,000 (shortage 3,000). So the old equilibrium is between $200 and $250 (a straight-line estimate gives about $237.50 and 8,750 tickets).
  • With S2 the equilibrium is $250 and 8,000.
  • So a decrease in supply raises the equilibrium price and lowers the equilibrium quantity.

4. (250, 9,000) → (250, 8,000): the price did not change but the quantity supplied fell, so it is a shift of the supply curve (S1 to S2). (250, 8,000) → (200, 7,000) on S2: the quantity fell because the price fell, so it is a movement along the supply curve.

When you draw it: price on the Y axis, quantity on the X axis.
memorize: Y axis = price, X axis = quantity. Always.
Equilibrium: $250, 8,000 tickets (Qd = Qs).
Fig 3-6: −1,000 at every price → supply shifts LEFT.
Supply decrease → price up, quantity down.
Same price, new quantity = shift; new price = movement along.

label: Q29–Q31
topic: US and Brazil PPFs: opportunity cost, comparative advantage, gains from trade
explain:
Slide 25 — three hand-drawn PPFs. In all graphs the vertical axis is parts (y) and the horizontal axis is sugar (x).

  • US PPF: x/20 + y/5 = 1. Max 20 sugar (if no parts) or 5 parts (if no sugar). The point (16 sugar, 1 part) is marked on the line. A dot is drawn above it, outside the line.
  • Brazil PPF: x/40 + y/4 = 1. Max 40 sugar or 4 parts.
  • "US and Brazil PPF Combined": both lines drawn together, plus a red line x/40 + y/5 = 1 from 5 parts (US max) to 40 sugar (Brazil max).

How to read a PPF equation x/a + y/b = 1: a = max of x, b = max of y. A point is on the PPF if x/a + y/b = 1, inside if < 1, outside (not reachable alone) if > 1.

Opportunity cost from a straight-line PPF: US can make 20 sugar OR 5 parts. So 1 part costs 20/5 = 4 sugar, and 1 sugar costs 5/20 = 1/4 part. This is the slide 24 "Step 1" table.

Comparative advantage = lower opportunity cost. Absolute advantage = can make more of it.

The deal on slide 24: US makes only parts (5), Brazil makes only sugar (40). US gives 2 parts and gets 16 sugar. Then US has (16 sugar, 3 parts) and Brazil has (24 sugar, 2 parts). Both points are outside their own PPFs, and both lie on the red "combined" line.

Everyday example: you cook faster, your friend cleans faster. Each does what costs them less, then you share. Both end up with more.
question:
The US PPF is x/20 + y/5 = 1 and the Brazil PPF is x/40 + y/4 = 1 (x = sugar, y = parts).

Q29. Find each country's maximum output of each good and the opportunity cost of one sugar and of one part in each country (Step 1 table).

Q30. Which country has the comparative advantage in each good? Which has the absolute advantage? What should each country specialize in, and how much is produced in total? Explain the red "combined" line x/40 + y/5 = 1.

Q31. Without trade the US consumes (16 sugar, 1 part). With trade the US gives 2 parts to Brazil and receives 16 sugar. (a) Is this trade acceptable to both countries? (b) Show that both countries are better off.
answer:
Q29. Maximums and opportunity costs

  • US: x/20 + y/5 = 1 → max 20 sugar or 5 parts.
  • Brazil: x/40 + y/4 = 1 → max 40 sugar or 4 parts.
US opportunity costBrazil opportunity cost
One sugar5/20 = 1/4 part4/40 = 1/10 part
One part20/5 = 4 sugars40/4 = 10 sugars

(The steepness of each PPF line, parts per sugar, is the "one sugar" row: US 1/4, Brazil 1/10.)

Q30. Comparative and absolute advantage

  • Sugar: Brazil 1/10 part < US 1/4 part → Brazil has the comparative advantage in sugar.
  • Parts: US 4 sugar < Brazil 10 sugar → the US has the comparative advantage in parts.
  • Absolute advantage: Brazil in sugar (40 > 20), US in parts (5 > 4).
  • Specialize: US makes only parts (5), Brazil makes only sugar (40). Total = 40 sugar + 5 parts.
  • The red line x/40 + y/5 = 1 joins 5 parts (US max) and 40 sugar (Brazil max). Its slope is 40 sugar per 5 parts = 8 sugar per part. Both after-trade bundles lie on it: US 16/40 + 3/5 = 0.4 + 0.6 = 1; Brazil 24/40 + 2/5 = 0.6 + 0.4 = 1.

Q31(a). Is the trade acceptable?

  • US gives up 2 parts. Each part costs the US 4 sugar, so it needs at least 2 × 4 = 8 sugar. It receives 16 > 8 → acceptable. (The slide writes "2 × (20/4) = 10"; by the Step 1 table it is 2 × (20/5) = 8. Either way 16 is enough.)
  • Brazil gives up 16 sugar. Each sugar costs Brazil 1/10 part, so it needs at least 16 × (4/40) = 1.6 parts. It receives 2 > 1.6 → acceptable.
  • The price is 16 sugar / 2 parts = 8 sugar per part, which is between the two opportunity costs (4 and 10). So the trade is possible.

Q31(b). Both better off

Produces with tradeGivesGetsConsumes with tradePPF test
US0 sugar, 5 parts2 parts16 sugar16 sugar, 3 parts16/20 + 3/5 = 1.4 > 1 → outside
Brazil40 sugar, 0 parts16 sugar2 parts24 sugar, 2 parts24/40 + 2/4 = 1.1 > 1 → outside
  • US: before trade (16, 1) is on its PPF (16/20 + 1/5 = 1). With 16 sugar, alone it could make only 5 × (1 − 16/20) = 1 part. With trade it has 3 parts: +2 parts, same sugar.
  • Brazil: with 24 sugar, alone it could make only 4 × (1 − 24/40) = 1.6 parts; with trade it has 2. Or: with 2 parts, alone it could have only 40 × (1 − 2/4) = 20 sugar; with trade it has 24 (+4 sugar).
  • Both countries consume a point outside their own PPF: "US could not reach (16, 3), Brazil could not reach (2, 24) before." So both are better off. Total consumption 16 + 24 = 40 sugar and 3 + 2 = 5 parts = total production.

US: 1 part = 4 sugar, 1 sugar = 1/4 part. Brazil: 1 part = 10 sugar, 1 sugar = 1/10 part.
Comparative adv: US → parts, Brazil → sugar. Total 40 sugar + 5 parts.
Deal 2 parts for 16 sugar = 8 sugar/part, inside 4–10 → works.
US min 8 sugar (slide says 10); Brazil min 1.6 parts.
After trade: US (16 sugar, 3 parts), Brazil (24 sugar, 2 parts), both outside own PPF, both on red line.
